readerTitle: Why you call the plumber your neighbor used
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관 수리업, 피자 가게) + 경제학 개념 (경험재·신뢰재 구분, Nelson 1970 / Darby & Karni 1973)
insight: 브랜드 신뢰는 고객이 확인할 수 없는 순간에 우리가 어떻게 행동할지에 대한 예측이며, 품질을 판단하기 어려운 상품일수록 가격의 더 큰 부분이 신뢰에 대한 대가다.
misconception: 신뢰는 '믿을 수 있는 업체'라고 광고하거나 가격을 낮추면 얻을 수 있다.

sources.text: Nelson, P. (1970). Information and Consumer Behavior. Journal of Political Economy, 78(2).
Darby, M. R. & Karni, E. (1973). Free Competition and the Optimal Amount of Fraud. Journal of Law and Economics, 16(1).
배관공, 피자 가게 사례와 가격은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 검색재·경험재 구분은 Nelson(1970), 신뢰재(credence goods) 개념은 Darby & Karni(1973)에서 나왔습니다. 카드 5에서는 논문 내용을 인용하지 않고 "economists sort purchases"로만 일반화해 적었습니다. 게시 전 표현이 원 개념과 맞는지 확인하세요.
훅의 "Many people call the second one"은 조사 수치가 아닌 설명용 서술입니다. 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요. 배관공 시급 $90/$120은 가상 수치입니다.
카드 7의 '신뢰는 쌓기는 느리고 잃기는 빠르다'는 일반적인 원리로만 적었고 특정 연구 수치를 붙이지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why you call the plumber your neighbor used
body: It's 9 p.m. and water is dripping through your kitchen ceiling. You find two plumbers online. One charges $90 an hour. The other charges $120, but your neighbor used them last year and said they were honest.
Many people call the second one. They aren't paying for better pipes. They're paying to worry less.

image.label: Dripping ceiling and a phone showing two plumber listings
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤의 부엌, 천장에서 물방울이 떨어지고 바닥에 양동이. 사람이 휴대폰을 들고 있고 화면에 배관공 두 곳이 나란히 보임: "$90/hr"와 "$120/hr · Your neighbor used them". 실제 업체 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Your plumbing business is new in town.
body: Your work is good and your prices are fair. But new customers keep choosing the older firm down the road. You have time and budget for one big move this quarter.

options.text: Cut your rates 20% below the older firm
options.feedback: You might win some price shoppers. But when buyers can't judge the work, a much lower price can look like a reason to worry, and it cuts what you keep from every job.

options.text: Give a fixed quote before starting, photograph the hidden work, and call before any change
options.feedback: This costs effort on every job, but it turns invisible good behavior into something customers can see and repeat to neighbors.

options.text: Run local ads calling yourself "the most trusted plumber in town"
options.feedback: Being known helps people find you. But saying you're trusted isn't evidence, and customers know any firm can print that line.

cards.title: The customer can't see inside the wall.
body: Even after the job, the homeowner may never know if the fix was done well, or whether it was needed at all.

So they aren't really choosing the best plumber. They're choosing the one they believe won't take advantage of them. A neighbor's story is evidence about exactly that. A low price or a bold slogan is not.

cards.title: Brand trust
body: **Brand trust** is a customer's belief that you will do right by them, especially in the moments they can't check.

A trusted name works as a shortcut. Instead of judging every detail, customers lean on what they've seen of your behavior before. That lowers the risk they feel, and lower risk is something people will pay extra for.

image.label: A balance scale: price on one side, worry on the other
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Price" 동전, 오른쪽 접시에 "Worry"라 적힌 먹구름. 신뢰받는 브랜드 쪽은 동전이 조금 더 무겁지만 먹구름이 훨씬 작게 그려짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Trust matters most when quality is hard to judge.
body: Economists sort purchases by when you can judge the quality:
list: **Before buying:** a chair you can sit in at the shop
**After buying:** a meal, a haircut, a hotel stay
**Maybe never:** a repair inside a wall, a tax return, a car service
cards.callout: The further down this list you sell, the more of your price is really a payment for trust.
cards.softwareNote: Software customers hand over data and daily work they can't inspect. Trust shows up in how you handle outages, security problems and billing mistakes, and whether you tell customers before they find out themselves.

cards.title: Trust is built where nobody is watching.
body: A plumber says, "This $15 part will fix it. You don't need a new boiler." A café throws out today's pastries at closing instead of selling them tomorrow.

Each is a moment where the business could quietly take advantage and doesn't. Trust grows when customers *find out* about those moments, so smart businesses make them visible: photos, plain explanations, prices agreed upfront.

image.label: Plumber showing a homeowner a photo of the repair on a tablet
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 배관공이 집주인에게 태블릿으로 벽 속 배관 수리 전후 사진을 보여주는 장면. 옆에 작은 부품 하나와 "$15" 가격표. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Trust is slow to build and quick to lose.
body: It takes many good moments to earn trust. One discovered shortcut can undo a lot of them, because customers tend to judge you by the worst thing they learn.

And trust can't rescue weak work. It gets people to try you, or give you one more chance. After that, the work itself has to keep earning it. Showing proof also takes time, so keep it short and useful.

cards.title: Now it's a pizza place.
body: Your best-selling pizza is known for its fresh mozzarella. This week your supplier ran out and sent a cheaper cheese. Most customers probably won't taste the difference.

options.text: Use it quietly. Nobody will notice for one week
options.feedback: You keep sales and margins this week. But if a regular or a staff member mentions it, you've shown what you do when no one is checking.

options.text: Keep selling it, but tell customers about the swap and take a little off the price
options.feedback: You give up a few dollars per pizza and gain a visible moment of honesty, the kind customers repeat to friends.

options.text: Take the pizza off the menu until the real cheese is back
options.feedback: This fully protects the promise, but you lose your best seller for a week when an honest note might have done the job.

cards.title: Trust is what customers believe you do when they can't check.
body: The harder your quality is to judge, the more customers are buying trust, not just the product. Earn it in the unseen moments, then let people see them.
**Try it today:** list one thing your customers can't check about your work. Find one simple way to show them you do it right.
